reviewRecords.title: More positive and more active: Effects of daily intergenerational engagement on emotion and physical activity
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Intergenerational engagement—here referring to time spent with younger family members—can promote health and happiness. Across adulthood, and particularly in later life, intergenerational engagement represents a potentially meaningful form of social involvement. Using intensive longitudinal , we investigated how intergenerational engagement is associated with daily emotional experience and physical activity.  In this study, 265 participants aged 23–92 completed a 9-day daily diary protocol assessing their intergenerational engagement and emotional experiences;  physical activity during this period was assessed via tracking steps taken and sedentary minutes.  Multilevel models revealed significant within-person associations between intergenerational engagement and both emotional experience and physical activity. On days older adult participants spent more time with younger family members, they reported greater high-arousal positive emotion (happiness, enthusiasm, excitement) during the day. Across the age span of the sample, on days participants spent more time with younger family members, they reported greater low-arousal positive emotion (contentment, relaxation, calm) before bed. Finally, both  metrics revealed greater physical activity on days with greater intergenerational engagement, whereas other social engagement was unassociated with steps taken or sedentary minutes. Discussion These findings highlight intergenerational engagement as a meaningful daily-life context for both positive emotional experiences and physical activity. For older adults in particular, intergenerational engagement may represent a naturally occurring pathway through which emotionally meaningful social ties support both emotional well-being and opportunities for everyday movement.

reviewRecords.title: The effects of physical and sensory activities on motor and cognitive functions in the aging brain: a review
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
authors: Sabrina Simplício de Araújo Romero Ferrari
Bárbara Querem Hapuque da Silva Linhares
reviewRecords.abstract: Brain aging characterized by progressive structural and functional changes, including atrophy of the hippocampus and frontal cortex, reduced neurogenesis and synaptogenesis, and disruptions in network connectivity, collectively impairing memory, attention, and executive functions. However, aging is increasingly recognized as a heterogeneous process, with variability in decline and preservation of certain cognitive capacities supported by compensatory mechanisms. Neuroplasticity plays a central role in mitigating age-related losses by enabling functional reorganization and maintaining neural connectivity. This integrative review synthesizes evidence on the effects of physical activity, sensory stimulation, and multisystem interventions on brain aging. Aerobic and multicomponent exercise programs, particularly those lasting 8–24 weeks, have been associated with improvements in hippocampal volume, executive function, and mobility. These benefits appear to be mediated by upregulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, vascular endothelial growth factor, lactate signaling, and cathepsin B, which support synaptic plasticity, neurogenesis, and cerebral perfusion. Sensory stimulation enhances neural processing through multisensory integration, strengthening connectivity within attentional and executive networks. Combined interventions that integrate motor, sensory, and cognitive components appear promising and may offer advantages over single‑domain approaches, although direct comparative evidence remains limited. Activities such as dance, proprioceptive training, and musical engagement exemplify sensorimotor integration, promoting cognitive reserve. In addition, emerging technologies, including virtual reality and brain-computer interfaces, further support personalized, neuroplasticity-driven rehabilitation. Together, these findings highlight sensorimotor integration as a central mechanism for preserving cognitive and functional capacity and promoting healthy brain aging.

reviewRecords.title: Community Exergaming and Maintenance-Related Outcomes in Older Adults: Multi-Wave Observational Evaluation
reviewRecords.abstract: Community exergaming may help older adults remain physically active by combining movement, enjoyment, and social interaction, but less is known about whether observed changes persist after supervised delivery ends in real-world community settings.  This study evaluated immediate and maintenance-related outcomes of the International Singapore Intergenerational National Games, a community-delivered exergaming program for older adults in Singapore. We examined positive mental health, intrinsic motivation, habit strength, physical activity, and exploratory implementation determinants aligned with the capability, opportunity, and motivation–behavior (COM-B) framework.  We conducted a multi-wave observational evaluation from October 2025 to January 2026 among 280 older adults recruited from 14 senior activity centers or active aging centers in Singapore. Assessments were conducted at baseline (T0), immediately after an 8-week supervised training phase (T1), after a 4-week unsupervised free-play phase (T2), and at a later follow-up for selected measures in 6 centers (T3). Immediate within-person changes were examined using 2-tailed paired t tests. Maintenance-related trajectories were examined using adjusted linear mixed-effects models. Exploratory analyses examined whether COM-B–aligned capability, opportunity, and motivation composites were associated with physical activity trajectories.  Participants had a mean age of 72.54 (SD 6.15) years, and 77.1% (216/280) were female. From T0 to T1, mean positive mental health increased from 55.19 (SD 9.79) to 57.59 (SD 8.70; Cohen dz =0.28; P dz =0.40; P dz =0.42; P P =.005), and intrinsic motivation remained higher at T2 (β=0.397, 95% CI .156-.638; P =.001) and T3 (β=0.305, 95% CI .009-.601; P =.04). Positive mental health was higher immediately after supervised training (β=4.140, 95% CI 2.169-6.111; P P P =.03), with no evidence of a sustained interaction at T2.  In this observational evaluation, positive mental health, intrinsic motivation, and habit strength were higher at T2 than at baseline among respondents with available follow-up data, and intrinsic motivation was also higher at the selected-center T3 follow-up. Because this study lacked a control group and attrition increased over time, these findings represent observed longitudinal trajectories rather than causal evidence of program effectiveness. Opportunity-related supports such as access, reminders, routines, staff facilitation, and peer participation may be useful when community exergaming transitions from supervised delivery to reduced-intensity free play, although this interpretation remains exploratory.

reviewRecords.title: Competent to care? Grandchild care and frailty trajectory among Chinese middle-aged and older adults through a person-environment fit lens
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: This study investigated how grandchild care intensity and community environment influenced frailty trajectories among Chinese middle-aged and older adults, examining whether effects vary by initial frailty status and are moderated by community environment.  Using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (2013, 2015, 2018) combined with 2011 community data, this study included 13,531 respondents (40,593 observations) across 442 communities. Marginal structural models with stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting were employed to mitigate selection bias. Weighted regressions with community-clustered robust standard errors were constructed, with subgroup analyses stratified by baseline frailty status (non-frail, pre-frail, frail).  While grandchild care showed a null overall effect in the general population, specific impacts varied significantly by baseline frailty status. Intensive caregiving significantly decelerated frailty progression for non-frail adults, whereas moderate caregiving accelerated longitudinal decline among frail adults. Caregiving showed non-significant impacts on frailty trajectory among pre-frail adults. A supportive community environment exerted protective main effects across all subgroups, with the frail group being most affected. It also magnified the protective effects of intensive caregiving on baseline frailty for the non-frail group. Discussion Using a person–environment fit perspective, this study reveals that the health impacts of grandchild care depend on the fit between individuals’ pre-existing health status and caregiving demands, and the role of community becomes more salient as competence declines. Findings highlight the critical need to prioritize vulnerable frail caregivers in health interventions and underscore community development as a key strategy for facilitating healthy aging.

reviewRecords.title: Mastery moderates the association between cumulative socioeconomic status risk and accelerated biological aging among middle-aged Black American women
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: This study examines how exposure to cumulative socioeconomic status (SES) risk in midlife shapes subsequent biological aging among Black American women and tests whether a sense of mastery moderates these associations.  Using longitudinal data from 334 middle-aged Black American women in the Family and Community Health Study (FACHS), we used hierarchical regression models to test our hypotheses and probed the interaction by estimating conditional differences between high and low mastery across levels of cumulative SES risk.  Cumulative SES risk was significantly associated with accelerated aging. After accounting for key environmental, psychosocial, behavioral, and biological confounders, each additional risk factor was associated with an increase in GrimAgeAccel of approximately 0.53 years (6.4 months). Among women with lower mastery, cumulative SES risk was positively and significantly associated with accelerated biological aging, with each additional SES risk factor associated with an increase of approximately 0.59 years (7.1 months) in GrimAge acceleration. Cumulative SES risk was not associated with accelerated aging among women with higher mastery. Discussion Consistent with stress process theory, higher mastery was associated with a weaker association between cumulative socioeconomic disadvantage and accelerated aging among middle-aged Black American women. Persistent SES-related disparities in biological aging indicate that upstream sociostructural determinants impose a chronic physiological burden that cannot be addressed by individual coping resources alone. Simultaneously bolstering psychosocial resources and addressing the structural conditions that necessitate such high levels of individual coping may be critical for promoting sustained, population-level improvements in healthy aging.

reviewRecords.title: Fairness decision-making in younger and older adults and associated neural indices
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Previous literature using the mini-ultimatum game (the mini-UG) suggests that older adults consider outcomes more than others’ intentions during fairness-related decision-making, whereas younger adults show the opposite pattern. Age-related declines in theory of mind (ToM) and executive functioning (EF) have been suggested as potential mechanisms underlying these age-related differences, but specific mechanisms remain unclear. The present work examines whether and how neural and behavioral factors known to be related to ToM and EF are associated with age-related differences in fairness processing. Method Thirty-six younger (Mage = 21.19, SDage = 3.14) and 36 older (Mage = 72.08, SDage = 5.87) participants completed both magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) anatomical brain scans and the mini-UG alongside behavioral measures of ToM and EF outside of the scanner. Volumes and cortical thickness of ToM- and EF-related brain regions were extracted. Computational modeling of participant mini-UG decisions estimated individuals’ tendencies to consider intention vs. outcome information.  Older adults relied more on outcomes than intention information, whereas younger adults showed the opposite pattern. Structural brain indices and behavioral measures did not mediate age-related differences in decision-making. However, dmPFC volumes moderated the age differences in decision-making, and EF, but not ToM, was positively associated with intention-based (vs. outcome-based) decisions across age groups. Discussion These findings extend prior work on age differences in intention-based vs. outcome-based fairness consideration by showing that dmPFC volume may be one factor contributing to age differences in related decisions.

reviewRecords.title: “I don’t know whether I really have choices”: a multiperspective and longitudinal exploration of healthcare choices of older adults with multimorbidity
reviewRecords.abstract: and  As the prevalence of multimorbidity among older adults is rising, challenges regarding their end-of-life healthcare choices are increasingly relevant. To address knowledge gaps regarding decision-making, we explored how older adults with multimorbidity, their relatives and involved healthcare professionals experienced end-of-life healthcare choices, how their experiences related to each other and how these choices occurred in interactions between them over time. Research Design and  We conducted a multiperspective, longitudinal, interview and observation study with a phenomenological and ethnographic approach. We followed nine six-month patient trajectories with eleven relatives and 58 healthcare professionals and conducted 73 observations of patient-healthcare professional interactions and 63 interviews.  The meaning of end-of-life healthcare choices of older people with multimorbidity was essentially understood as an ongoing, entangled, existential and relational process, shaped by, yet also transcending, healthcare contexts. This process was characterized by four tensions: (i) the experience of not having a choice, but making decisions nonetheless; (ii) the existential experience and the medical gaze; (iii) the importance of relatives and their limited role in healthcare; and (iv) navigating fragmented healthcare with interrelated conditions.  Healthcare professionals’ limited insight into patients’ and relatives’ personal, existential perspectives and relational contexts calls for a better exploration of their lifeworld to ensure the best possible alignment of healthcare decisions with patients’ and relatives’ needs and values. Older adults with multimorbidity are inadequately supported by fragmented healthcare systems, and efforts to improve this should consider existential, relational and systemic factors.

reviewRecords.title: Prevalence and factors associated with malnutrition in critically ill elderly patients: a retrospective cohort study
reviewRecords.abstract: Malnutrition is a common but often under-recognized condition in critically ill older adults. Age-related physiological decline, including reduced nutritional reserve and increased vulnerability to stress, may exacerbate its impact; however, data focusing specifically on elderly intensive care unit (ICU) populations remain limited. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of malnutrition and identify associated factors in critically ill elderly patients.  We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients aged ≥ 60 years admitted to the medical ICU, Faculty of Medicine, Chiang Mai University, Thailand, between 1 January 2022 and 31 December 2023. Malnutrition was defined using the Nutrition Triage 2013 (NT2013) tool. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify factors associated with malnutrition, reported as adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).  Among 411 patients, 41.4% were malnourished at ICU admission. Compared with non-malnourished patients, those with malnutrition had greater illness severity (APACHE II 22 [IQR 18, 25] vs. 19 [IQR 15, 23], p p p p = 0.021), higher total bilirubin (aOR 1.12, 95% CI 1.01–1.24, p = 0.039), lower serum albumin level (aOR 0.48, 95% CI 0.34–0.67, p p  Malnutrition is highly prevalent among critically ill elderly patients and is associated with greater illness severity and increased ICU mortality. Early identification through systematic nutritional screening and appropriate management, particularly in patients with identified factors associated with malnutrition, may help mitigate adverse outcomes.

reviewRecords.title: Intergenerational Queer Trajectories : Friendship and Connectedness among Younger and Older LGBTQ+ People in Ireland
reviewRecords.abstract: This study examines intergenerational LGBTQ + friendships in Ireland, considering how queer understandings of time and ageing inform these relationships. Reflexive thematic analysis of life history interviews with seven younger (18-35) and seven older (60+) LGBTQ+ individuals revealed how shared queer experiences such as coming out, “gay age,” and relived adolescence create commonality and connection despite age differences. These friendships are also shaped through intergenerational exchange and “role modelling,” with LGBTQ+ knowledge and histories countering narratives like the “lonely old gay man” and offering alternative modes of queer ageing and living. While challenges arise from negative stereotypes, distinct historical contexts, and barriers to interaction, participants emphasise the sense of mutual understanding, historical connectedness, and hope for the future that underpins these bonds. Together, these findings illuminate what we term “intergenerational queer trajectories”: nonnormative life pathways involving shared queer experiences, histories, and imagined futures through which LGBTQ+ individuals connect across generations.

reviewRecords.title: Who Do You Trust? Demographic Patterns in Vaccine Hesitancy among Older Adults in a Rural State
reviewRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
reviewRecords.abstract: Older adults are at increased risk for complications from vaccine-preventable diseases, yet many remain undervaccinated. This study examined demographic variability in vaccination hesitancy among older adults in a rural state and the potentially mediating role of trust uncertainty. A cross-sectional survey of a random sample of 739 adults aged 65+ in North Dakota was conducted from May to July 2022. Using bootstrapped mediation analyses, we assessed whether trust uncertainty mediated the relationships between demographic characteristics and vaccine hesitancy and acceptance.  showed uncertainty about whom to trust was a significant predictor of both higher vaccine hesitancy and lower vaccine acceptance. Uncertainty about whom to trust fully mediated the relationship between rurality and vaccine hesitancy, and between education and vaccine acceptance. Political leaning and physical health were also partially mediated through uncertainty about whom to trust. These findings highlight the role of trust in shaping vaccine attitudes and the need for tailored communication strategies that address information uncertainty.

reviewRecords.title: Identifying Contextual Factors affecting Hospital In Home Program Implementation within the Veterans Health Administration
reviewRecords.abstract: and  Understanding the factors that enable or hinder successful implementation is essential for improving patient outcomes. Hospital in Home (HiH) programs provide hospital-level care in patients' homes to reduce hospitalization, enhance satisfaction, and improve resource use. Within the Veterans Health Administration (VHA), 14 sites have implemented HiH programs, yet limited research has examined implementation within a large integrated system. This study identifies factors that can support or hinder HiH implementation. Research Design and  We conducted interviews with 48 key informants across 14 VHA HiH sites. Guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) 2.0, we applied directed content analysis using a priori constructs, then developed site-level matrices to summarize findings and compare patterns across sites.  We identified 18 CFIR constructs—nine that primarily facilitated implementation and nine mixed factors that acted as both facilitators and barriers. Key facilitators included two Individual-level factors (HiH lead capability and motivation, team motivation), one Innovation factor (relative advantage of HiH), and four Implementation Process factors (planning, teaming, reflecting and evaluating, adapting). Mixed factors were mostly within the inner setting, reflecting medical center context, along with two Individual-level mixed factors (leader and recipient motivation).  HiH programs hold strong potential to transform care for older adults, but success depends on addressing barriers and leveraging facilitators, particularly within the inner setting. Understanding key implementation determinants can enhance adoption, improve outcomes, and strengthen healthcare delivery.

reviewRecords.title: Medicare Enrollment Literacy Among First-Time Black Beneficiaries: Insights From a Mixed-Methods Study
reviewRecords.abstract: and  Limited Medicare literacy contributes to suboptimal plan selection and disparities in coverage outcomes among older adults, particularly in historically underserved communities. This study examined Medicare enrollment literacy, information access, and decision-making experiences among first-time Black Medicare beneficiaries in Southeast Queens, New York, using a convergent mixed- design. Research Design and  Quantitative data were collected through a community-based survey of first-time Medicare beneficiaries (N = 93). Descriptive statistics assessed Medicare literacy across a 15-item scale and examined information sources, decision support, and plan selection patterns. Qualitative data were obtained through three focus groups and four individual interviews (N = 16) with community navigators and Medicare enrollment professionals and were analyzed using thematic analysis. Document analysis examined the clarity, readability, and cultural relevance of commonly used Medicare materials.  More than half of participants demonstrated low Medicare literacy, and fewer than half reported confidence in comparing plans, understanding coverage differences, and estimating out-of-pocket costs. Most participants received assistance with enrollment decisions. Qualitative findings identified five themes: complexity and information overload, reliance on informal support networks, digital navigation barriers, confusion about coverage and costs, and the importance of trust and culturally relevant communication. Document analysis indicated that many materials were complex and relied heavily on insurance terminology, with limited cultural tailoring.  Limited Medicare literacy reflects both individual knowledge gaps and systemic barriers. Enhancing culturally responsive outreach, simplifying materials, and expanding community-based decision support may improve equitable enrollment outcomes.

reviewRecords.title: Searching for Answers: Health Literacy and Digital Navigation in Midlife and Older Adults
reviewRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
reviewRecords.abstract: As digital, internet-based health communication becomes more common, understanding the factors influencing midlife and older adults’ ability to navigate online resources is essential. This study investigated whether health literacy interacts with communication format to affect health search performance. Seventy-eight community-dwelling midlife and older adults classified as having high or low health literacy using the Newest Vital Sign completed a counterbalanced print- and internet-based health search task. A 2 × 2 mixed-factorial analysis of variance revealed that both lower health literacy and the internet format were associated with poorer task accuracy and greater task completion time. Contrary to expectation, the influence of task format on performance did not disproportionately affect individuals with low health literacy. Findings suggest that both health literacy and communication formats independently influence midlife and older adults’ ability to accurately and efficiently retrieve health information. These  underscore the need for digital health literacy assessments and the development of interventions to support access to digital health information among aging adults.

reviewRecords.title: A New Tool to Assess the Person-Centeredness of Research Measures: The Person-Centered Measure Evaluation Tool (PC-MET)
reviewRecords.abstract: No tool exists to assess whether research measures themselves are consistent with principles of person-centeredness.  This project developed a tool to assess the extent of person-centeredness employed in the development, content, and application of research measure development in the context of measures relevant to persons living with dementia and/or their caregivers.  Literature review and expert input informed the development of the tool; pilot testing assessed interrater reliability and rater acceptability.  The tool includes six criteria (each with three subcategories): Co-Creation, Accommodation, Incorporation, Biopsychosocial-Cultural Components, Pragmatism, and Systemic Focus. Kappa agreement was substantial or better (0.61–1.00) for most (16/18) subcategories and for all six criteria (0.74–1.00). Raters found the tool easy to understand and score and the criteria to be relevant and complete.  The resulting tool—named the Person-Centered Measure Evaluation Tool (PC-MET)—can reliably critique existing measures and guide the development of new measures.

reviewRecords.title: A meta-ethnography of staff experiences of raising concerns about quality and safety in residential aged care
reviewRecords.abstract: and  Speaking up about quality and safety issues can protect older people and support learning in health and social care systems. In aged care, staff work in diverse roles to deliver care to residents with complex care needs. This meta-ethnography aimed to synthesise evidence on staff experiences of raising concerns about quality and safety in long-term residential aged care. Research Design and  We included qualitative studies examining staff experiences of speaking up, incident reporting, and whistleblowing. Five databases were searched. The seven phases of meta-ethnography were used to translate first and second order constructs into third order constructs and a line-of-argument synthesis.  Thirteen articles of 11 studies were synthesised to reveal four third order constructs: 1. Sensemaking a concern, 2. Organisational cultures determine how they are voiced, heard and respond to, 3. Systemic resources shape and constrain possibilities for voicing, and 4. Normalisation of poor care and loss of moral agency in organisations that respond with indifference. Raising concerns was a dynamic, recursive process encompassing phases of recognising, voicing, and organisational responding. Where quality and safety issues were normalised, individualised, or met with limited action, staff described moral distress, disengagement, and, in some cases, exit from the organisation or sector.  Raising concerns in residential aged care is a dynamic process shaped by interrelated individual, organisational and systemic factors. Speaking up interventions need to go beyond skills training to address phases of recognising care quality issues and how organisations respond when they are raised.

reviewRecords.title: Beyond Attendance: Participation and Relational Work in Planned Group Recreational Activities in a Long-Term Care Village Setting
reviewRecords.abstract: and  Person-centered care (PCC) has shaped dementia care reforms and informed innovative long-term care models such as care villages. Recreational activities are often seen as a site where PCC is enacted, yet little empirical work has examined how participation in structured activities is enabled, mediated, and constrained through everyday social, relational, and organizational dynamics. This study examines how participation in structured group activities was produced in a care village. Research Design and  An ethnographic study was conducted in Canada’s first publicly funded care village, drawing on 100 hours of participant observation, 12 staff interviews, and informal resident conversations. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis.  Participation varied across activity types and residents’ fluctuating comfort, stamina, and readiness. For many residents, participation was not simply an individual decision, but was scaffolded through staff invitation, accessible information, relational familiarity, and individualized encouragement. It also depended on logistical and organizational conditions, including preparation, transportation, staffing coordination, and role boundaries. These findings show that participation was relationally and organizationally produced rather than simply a matter of resident preference or program design.  Structured activities can support meaningful engagement when sustained by relational, logistical, and organizational work. The findings clarify how PCC commitments such as choice, autonomy, and inclusion are enacted through activity systems, while highlighting the labor-intensive conditions required for more equitable participation. These insights have implications for staffing, coordination, and activity provision in care villages and long-term care settings.

reviewRecords.title: Blunted Diurnal Cortisol Slope as a Risk Marker for 9-Year Executive Function Decline: Amplification by Daily Stress and Worry Severity
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Cortisol dysregulation, reflective of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis dysregulation, has been linked to executive functioning (EF) decline. However, substantial effect-size heterogeneity across studies highlights the potential role of psychosocial moderators. We investigated whether the severity of perceived daily stressors and chronic worry moderated the relationships between baseline cortisol dysregulation and 9-year EF.  Community adults (N = 1,617) completed four-day, four-times-daily salivary cortisol sampling and an eight-day interview-driven daily diary at baseline. Three cortisol metrics were computed: area under the curve (AUC), cortisol awakening response (CAR), and diurnal cortisol slope (DCS). Linear mixed models determined whether daily stressor or chronic worry severity moderated associations between baseline cortisol metrics and 9-year EF, adjusting for baseline EF.  Daily stressor severity significantly moderated the relationship between DCS–but not AUC or CAR–and 9-year EF (Cohen’s d = 0.113). Flatter DCS was associated with poorer EF across all stressor severity levels, although the observed numerical attenuation at higher severity was not statistically confirmed. Chronic worry severity was significantly associated with lower 9-year EF across all cortisol metrics and significantly moderated the CAR-to-EF relationship (d = –0.176). Exploratory analyses suggested that a flatter DCS was associated with worse EF at higher worry severity, but this interaction was not significant. Discussion These outcomes broadly align with moderation, not mediation, suggesting that psychosocial stress and worry can amplify, rather than yield, cortisol-linked relationships with EF. Pending replication, HPA-axis circadian modulation and chronic worry severity can indicate viable targets for prevention research.

reviewRecords.title: Living Well at Home With Dementia: Home Modifications, Caregiving Duration, and Subjective Well-Being
reviewRecords.abstract: Supporting people with dementia to live well at home requires balancing safety with emotional well-being. Although home modifications are promoted to enhance independence, their implications for subjective well-being remain unclear.  This study examined associations between home modifications, caregiving duration, and subjective well-being among community-dwelling older adults with dementia, informed by the Ecological Theory of Aging.  Using data from five NHATS waves (2015–2019), we conducted pooled cross-sectional regression analyses using repeated person-wave observations ( N = 340 individuals; mostly 70–84 years, 54% women). Regression models assessed associations between home modifications, caregiving duration, and subjective well-being, including self-efficacy and positive affect.  Home modifications were associated with lower levels of both self-efficacy and positive affect. Longer caregiving duration attenuated the negative association between home modifications and positive affect. Findings highlight that physical and social environments jointly shape adaptation experiences, underscoring the need for personalized, dignity-preserving dementia care.

reviewRecords.title: Response consistency and response time across later life stages: Evidence from a factorial survey on housing decisions
reviewRecords.abstract: and  Factorial surveys are increasingly used in gerontological research to study complex decision-making in later life. While prior work has demonstrated their feasibility among older adults, less is known about how response behaviour varies across later-life stages and how response time relates to response consistency, particularly among the oldest old. Research Design and  Data are drawn from a factorial survey on housing decisions conducted with a convenience sample of adults aged 50 to 99 years in Germany (N = 266). Response inconsistency was operationalised as a respondent-level measure based on residual variation in vignette evaluations. Regression and interaction analyses were used to examine age-related patterns and the relationship between response time and response inconsistency.  Response time increased with age. Response inconsistency did not vary across most age groups but was higher among the oldest respondents. No statistically robust association between response time and response inconsistency was observed, and interaction effects were not significant. Exploratory analyses indicated that age-related differences in inconsistency were detectable only within a limited range of response times.  The findings emphasise the importance of differentiating between stages of later life when assessing survey response behaviour. They suggest that response pace and response consistency capture distinct dimensions that should not be treated as interchangeable indicators of data quality. By focusing on age-specific patterns, the study contributes to a more differentiated interpretation of response behaviour in gerontological survey research.

reviewRecords.title: Constraint or Warning? Health Shocks and Dietary Habits Among Older Adults in China
reviewRecords.abstract: Health shocks may reshape health behaviors in later life, yet their implications for dietary habits remain insufficiently understood. Using six waves of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey from 2002 to 2018, this study examines the association between serious illness episodes and dietary diversity among Chinese older adults. The  show that health shocks are significantly associated with lower dietary diversity. This association remains stable across sensitivity analyses. Heterogeneity analyses further indicate that the negative association is stronger among the oldest adults and those with a higher chronic disease burden. Mechanism analyses suggest that financial condition, physiological functioning, and outdoor activity partly account for the association. These findings suggest that, among older adults in China, health shocks may operate more as constraints that reduce the capacity to maintain diverse diets. Post-illness care should therefore integrate nutritional support, functional recovery, and community-based assistance, especially for older adults with greater health vulnerability.

reviewRecords.title: Metabolomic Profiling of Telomere Length: Associations with Aging-related Phenotypes and Modifiable Lifestyle Factors in Chinese Older Adults
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Telomere length (TL) is a well-established biomarker of cellular senescence, yet the metabolic profile of TL and its associations with aging-related phenotypes and responses to modifiable lifestyle factors remain unclear.  TL was measured using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) in 282 participants from the West China Health and Aging Cohort (WCHAC). Plasma metabolites were analyzed using Liquid Chromatography-tandem Mass Spectrometry. TL-associated metabolic signatures (Met-TL) were identified through elastic net regression models. Associations between Met-TL and aging-related phenotypes and modifiable lifestyle factors were evaluated using linear and logistic regression models in a larger, non-overlapping sample of 5,957 WCHAC participants. Furthermore, we employed mediation analysis to explore the mediating effects of Met-TL between lifestyle factors and aging-related diseases.  We identified a plasma metabolite signature comprising 26 metabolites explaining 17.5% of TL variance. Met-TL significantly associated with aging-related phenotypes (44 Bonferroni-corrected associations) and modifiable lifestyle factors (4 associations). Notably, Met-TL showed robust associations with steatohepatitis and hepatic biomarkers. Mediation analysis revealed that Met-TL partially explained the protective association between healthy lifestyle and steatohepatitis, with a mediation proportion of 8.2%.  These findings provide novel insights into the metabolic profile of TL in older adults. The Met-TL may serve as a promising biomarker of cellular aging, particularly in identifying liver dysfunction, facilitating the development of personalized aging monitoring and anti-aging intervention strategies.

reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Mounting evidence points to the protective role of adult child education in older parents' health, including their risk of ADL and IADL difficulties. Yet, little is known whether this association varies cross-nationally due to contextual differences in intergenerational transfers, family dynamics, and other factors. This study examines the relationship between adult child education and parents’ functional health outcomes across countries, using comparable population-based datasets.  We used harmonized data from seven population-based studies accessed through the Gateway to Global Aging Data. Our analytic sample included 88,683 adults 60 years and older from 24 countries. We estimated and meta-analyzed associations between adult child education and respondents’ (parents’) difficulty with basic and instrumental activities of daily living (ADL and IADLs), controlling for respondents’ own education and other socio-demographic characteristics. We also considered heterogeneity across parent and child demographics (e.g. parent gender, child gender).  Across all studies, each additional year of education averaged across adult children was associated with a 3% lower risk of difficulty with both ADLs (95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 0.95, 0.98) and IADLs (95% CI: 0.95, 0.98). Statistical heterogeneity appeared to be driven by one study (e.g. I2 = 78.94% when the study was included vs. I2 = 0.04% when excluded).  suggest limited heterogeneity across demographic subgroups.  “Upward” intergenerational benefits of higher adult child education for parents’ late-life ADL and IADL difficulties appear to be relatively consistent across a range of global settings. Further research is needed to uncover the mechanisms driving these cross-national associations.

reviewRecords.title: Unequal Embodiment: Racial and Ethnic Heterogeneity in the Predictors and Age-Related Health Outcomes Associated with Accelerated Biological Aging
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: This study investigates whether life-course socioeconomic exposures are similarly associated with accelerated biological aging across racial and ethnic groups, and whether accelerated biological aging predicts health outcomes equivalently across groups.  Data came from the Health and Retirement Study (2016-2022). Accelerated biological age was derived from 22 blood-based biomarkers from the 2016 Venous Blood Study. We used linear regression models with interactions between race/ethnicity and life-course exposures (childhood adversity and adult/midlife socioeconomic status (SES)) to assess group differences in accelerated aging. Linear, multinomial, and logistic regression models with interactions between accelerated biological age and race/ethnicity were used to assess group differences in health outcomes. We examined differences by foreign-born status among Hispanic adults.  Associations between life-course exposures, accelerated biological aging, and health varied by race/ethnicity. Compared to non-Hispanic White adults, childhood health and adversity were not associated with accelerated biological aging for non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic adults, and among these groups, higher midlife SES did not decelerate biological aging. The association between accelerated biological age and health outcomes varied by race/ethnicity; accelerated biological age was less predictive among non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic adults. Among Hispanic adults, foreign-born status was a significant moderator: increased biological age was more strongly linked to morbidity among foreign-born individuals.  The processes linking life-course conditions to biological aging, and biological aging to later-life health, do not translate uniformly across racial/ethnic groups. Future research should explore the sources of heterogeneity in life-course exposures and the mechanisms by which biological age translates into health outcomes.

reviewRecords.title: Hypertensive crisis in the elderly: epidemiological, clinical and outcome: EDEN-47 study
reviewRecords.abstract: PURPOSE: To define the frequency and annual rate of hypertensive crisis in older patients attending emergency department (ED), the sociodemographic and baseline patient profile, and clinical characteristics and long-term outcome of the hypertensive crisis episode. We also looked for differences between men and women. : This was a retrospective analysis of the multipurpose EDEN cohort, which recruited during 1-week period all patients aged 65 years who visited the ED of 52 Spanish public hospitals covering 19.3% of Spanish population. Demographic, social, baseline and clinical data of the episode of hypertensive crisis were recorded. Estimations of annual incidence were made, in general and through patient age. Outcome consisted of 1-year post-discharge combined adverse event (revisit to ED, hospitalization, or death). Comparison between men and women were performed in unadjusted and adjusted models. : There were 186 cases of hypertensive crises among the 25,557 patients included in the EDEN cohort. The relative frequency of hypertensive crisis was 0.73% of ED visits (95%CI 0.63-0.84), with 0.56% (0.44-0.72) in men and 0.87% (0.73-1.04) in women (OR for men 0.64, 0.47-0.87), and annual rate of hypertensive crisis in Spanish older population was 429 cases per 100.000 inhabitants (95%CI 371-493), with 341 (267-436) in men and 493 (413-590) in women (OR for men 0.69, 0.51-0.94). Patients with hypertensive crisis had better baseline health status than the rest of the older patients attending the ED, with cardiovascular comorbidity being frequent (previously known hypertension in 88.2%) and with 22% having additional acute diagnoses on top of the hypertensive crisis. Hospitalization was needed in 7.5% of cases (0.5% in intensive care unit) and in-hospital mortality was observed in 2 cases (1.1%). Combined adverse events 1 year after discharge accounted for 57.9% of patients, with 65.6% in men and 52.5% in women (adjusted HR 1.61, 1.01-2.57). : Hypertensive crises are more frequent in older women than men and they present a worse profile at baseline and higher severity than men. Nonetheless, men with hypertensive crisis may have a worse long-term prognosis compared to women, highlighting the need for targeted post-discharge monitoring strategies in this subgroup.

reviewRecords.title: Early life predictors of subjective cognitive function in older age: Emerging longitudinal associations over six decades
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Self-rated memory impairment is common in older age and has been related to  cognitive decline and dementia. Recently, there has been growing interest in early-life predictors of late-life cognition, but research has been limited due to the absence of data spanning the entire lifespan. The present study investigated whether psychological health, social well-being, socioeconomic status (SES), and cognitive abilities at age 10 and 13 predicted subjective memory almost six decades later.  Psychological health, social well-being, SES, and cognitive abilities were measured with standardized tests and questionnaires at age 10 and 13. Subjective memory, anxiety, and depressive symptoms were measured with the Prospective and Retrospective Memory Questionnaire (PRMQ) and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) at age 67 (n = 625).  In a longitudinal autoregressive structural equation model (SEM), higher levels of psychological health at age 13 predicted lower levels of subjective memory at age 67. This association was independent of current anxiety and depressive symptoms. The model did not provide sufficient support that social well-being, SES, cognitive ability, and school performance at age 13 predicted subjective memory at age 67. Additional analysis revealed that psychological health at age 13, but not at age 10, and anxiety symptoms at age 67 uniquely predicted subjective memory at age 67. Discussion These findings extend prior research by showing that psychological health is a robust predictor of subjective memory. Interventions targeting early-life psychological health may help identify individuals with different prospective cognitive outcomes in later life.

reviewRecords.title: Reproductive life course histories and menopausal outcomes at midlife: Evidence from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Menopause is a heterogeneous transition that varies in timing and type, yet population-based research rarely considers how reproductive life course experiences shape menopausal outcomes. This study examines whether reproductive timing, reproductive history, and reproductive health across adolescence and adulthood are associated with menopausal status, early menopause, and surgical menopause at midlife.  Using data from women in Waves I–VI of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), we constructed reproductive life course histories including pubertal timing, pregnancy and parity, reproductive complications, and gynecologic conditions. Menopausal outcomes at Wave VI included menopausal status, early menopause (before age 40), and surgical menopause. Survey-weighted logistic regression models estimated associations between reproductive characteristics and menopausal outcomes, adjusting for socioeconomic context and cumulative reproductive stress. Stratified analyses by pregnancy history assessed whether associations with gynecologic pathology were independent of fertility history.  At Wave VI (mean age 44), 18% of women were postmenopausal. Among them, 69% reported surgical menopause and 60% experienced menopause before age 40, indicating a substantial prevalence of non-natural and early transitions. Pregnancy and parity were consistently associated with menopausal outcomes, whereas reproductive timing showed more limited associations. Gynecologic pathology was strongly associated with early and surgical menopause independent of pregnancy history. Discussion Menopause emerges as a life course process shaped by reproductive histories and midlife reproductive health. The high prevalence of early and surgical menopause underscores the importance of examining heterogeneous pathways to menopausal timing and type in population-based research.

reviewRecords.title: Seeing no way out: Exploring the connection between internalized caregiver stigma, entrapment, suicidal ideation and depressive symptoms among Canadian informal caregivers
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Informal caregivers’ beliefs about caregiving for older adults (i.e. caregiver stigma) are associated with suicidal ideation and poor mental health. As only few studies have studied this association, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study analyzed whether caregiver stigma is associated with suicidal ideation and depression via feelings of entrapment.  Canadian long-term caregivers of adults aged 60+ years (N = 175, 18-95+ years) were surveyed online with the internalized caregiver stigma scale (self-devaluing (negative) and self-affirming (positive) stereotypes, attitudes, and behaviors), about their feelings of entrapment (short entrapment scale), depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation (PHQ-9). Regression analysis with robust standard errors and causal mediation analysis with bootstrapped standard errors were conducted.  Regression models indicated entrapment and negative care stigma were associated with more depressive symptoms, and entrapment with higher suicidal ideation. Significant indirect effects of positive and negative caregiver stigma components on suicidal ideation as well as depressive symptoms via entrapment were found in the causal mediation models. Additionally, positive caregiver stigma interacted with entrapment in the model for suicidal ideation. Discussion This study highlighted that the path from negative caregiver self-stigma to a higher level of suicidal ideation and depressive symptoms seems to be rooted through increased feelings of entrapment. Conversely, the self-affirming form of caregiver stigma had a hidden protective effect for both outcomes via lower feelings of entrapment. Targeting care-related stigma may thus help reduce the danger of negative mental health outcomes among caregivers of older adults by changing their constricting perception of being trapped.

reviewRecords.title: Enhancing Participation in an Undergraduate Aging Research Training Program
reviewRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
reviewRecords.abstract: Research teams addressing inequalities in aging benefit from diverse perspectives that can strengthen the scientific rigor of the research. We developed a mentored research program to encourage diversity in population health aging research. Our program, Advancing Health Equity and Diversity (AHEaD), focused on reducing barriers to application and enrollment. We received robust interest in the program, including nearly 4,500 applications over 5 years (2021–2025), and welcomed 45 participants. Participants positively evaluated the application process. We received outcomes data on 40/45 participants as of September 2025, and 35/40 participants (87.5%) had engaged in research/employment, or were in the process of applying or had matriculated in graduate school. In summary, strategies designed to enhance participation and lower barriers to application yielded a high interest in our AHEaD program, and this interest was linked to high engagement in further research, employment, and education in population aging research.

reviewRecords.title: Reconstructing Identity in the Shadow of Dementia: Narrative Identity Processes Among Adult Child Caregivers
reviewRecords.abstract: Caring for a parent with dementia constitutes a profound relational and existential transition for adult children, extending beyond functional caregiving demands to processes of identity negotiation and reconstruction. Although extensive research has documented caregiver burden, psychological distress, and health consequences in dementia caregiving, comparatively little attention has been devoted to the narrative mechanisms through which caregivers sustain a coherent sense of self. Drawing on narrative identity theory, ambiguous loss theory, and the concept of biographical disruption, this qualitative narrative study explored how adult children construct identity narratives while caring for a parent with dementia. Semi-structured narrative interviews with 21 caregivers were analyzed using a holistic narrative approach informed by narrative selection theory. Four dominant narrative identity patterns emerged: management narratives emphasizing control and competence, growth narratives framing caregiving as personal transformation, protective boundary narratives focusing on identity differentiation, and fracture and alienation narratives. These narratives functioned as adaptive mechanisms for negotiating agencies, continuity, and moral positioning under conditions of chronic relational loss. The findings extend dementia caregiving research by conceptualizing caregiving as an ongoing narrative identity project rather than solely a burden experience, highlighting the central role of meaning-making, cultural expectations, and epistemic agency in caregiver adaptation.

reviewRecords.title: Termination of SNAP Emergency Allotments increased food insufficiency among older adults
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: We examined how the nationwide termination of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) Emergency Allotments (EA) affected food insufficiency among older adults aged 60 and older, a group with high rates of nutrition-sensitive disease conditions and low SNAP uptake.  Using Household Pulse Survey data on older adult households with incomes below 200 percent of the federal poverty level, we applied a stacked difference-in-differences design to compare food insufficiency within three-month windows before and after EA termination.  Food insufficiency rose by 1.5 percentage points among older adult households overall and by 3.3 percentage points among older adults living alone, with no significant change among those not living alone. The difference in effects between those living alone and those not living alone was not statistically significant at conventional levels (p = 0.091). Sensitivity analyses restricting to self-identified SNAP recipients or varying the analytic window yielded consistent . Discussion These findings indicate that the loss of higher SNAP benefits substantially increased food hardship among low-income older adults post-COVID, underscoring the need for adequate benefit levels.

reviewRecords.title: Volunteering Experience and Intentions Among Older Adults in Italy: Evidence From a Large Quota Sample
reviewRecords.abstract: The present study investigates volunteering experience and intentions in a large quota sample of older Italian adults aged 60–74 stratified by geographic area and sex (N = 700), focusing on sociodemographic factors, Self-Determination Theory (SDT), and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB).  showed that 35.1% of respondents engaged in formal volunteering in the 12 months prior to the study. Using logistic regressions, we found that past participation is significantly associated with higher education and income, better self-reported health, frequent religious attendance, intrinsic motivation, and perceived behavioral control. Conversely, probit ordinal regression showed that intentions to volunteer are primarily driven by prior experience, subjective norms, positive attitudes, integrated and introjected regulation. Our findings highlight the interplay between socioeconomic resources and socio-cognitive processes related to volunteering among older adults in the Italian context and can inform policies and interventions that promote active aging and well-being by addressing psychological barriers and motivators.

reviewRecords.title: Connected and Eager to Learn: Digital Skills, Challenges, and Unmet Needs of Older Adults in Long-Term Care Facilities
reviewRecords.abstract: This study explores the digital skills and challenges of older adults living in long-term care settings. We conducted 14 focus group interviews with 59 residents in Switzerland, with an average age of 80, to identify the competencies they possess and the skills they lack. Participants described using digital tools to stay connected and maintain autonomy. However, they also reported barriers such as cognitive limitations, rapid technological changes, and difficulty managing digital information. Despite these challenges, many expressed interest in improving their digital abilities. Our findings show that older adults in care settings want to engage with technology but often lack the necessary support. We conclude that providing hands-on training, simplifying digital interfaces, and offering ongoing assistance can reduce frustration, build confidence, and help residents manage daily tasks more independently.

reviewRecords.title: Building Student Skills and Belonging as Geroscience and Gerojustice Researchers Through a Longevity and Aging Research Education Program: A Qualitative Analysis
reviewRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
reviewRecords.abstract: Addressing cumulative health disparities across the lifespan requires a scientific workforce trained at the intersection of geroscience and gerojustice. By integrating holistic academic and social support, an interdisciplinary Longevity and Aging minor, and scaffolded intramural and extramural research mentorship, the Katies for Aging Research and Equity (KARE) Program at St. Catherine University positions students to succeed as future aging researchers. To evaluate student growth, focus group transcripts, written reflections, Individual Development Plans, and student advocacy testimonials were examined. The qualitative analysis revealed three interconnected themes defining the scholar experience: (1) scholarly skill development, (2) belonging to a scholarly community, and (3) reframing longevity and aging. Beyond individual scholar growth, the KARE program has catalyzed broader institutional shifts, driving student-led research advocacy, interdisciplinary curriculum integration, and university-wide age-friendly initiatives. We offer a model for training future researchers to address complex health disparities in the intersecting fields of geroscience and gerojustice.

reviewRecords.title: The National Archive of Computerized Data on Aging (NACDA) Portal: Variable-level discovery and custom metadata and data extraction for aging research
reviewRecords.abstract: and  Population aging has intensified demand for data infrastructure that supports life-course, cohort, and within-person research using longitudinal surveys. However, traditional file-centric dissemination and the growing number and diversity of aging data collections have complicated secondary analysis, limiting researchers’ ability to locate comparable measures, evaluate cross-wave continuity, and assemble cross-study analytic datasets. To address these challenges, we introduced the National Archive of Computerized Data on Aging (NACDA) Portal, a variable-level metadata discovery and extraction platform developed by NACDA in collaboration with Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research and Colectica. Research Design and  Established in 2019, the portal integrates 17 longitudinal aging studies encompassing over 210,000 variables. Organized by concept and harmonized metadata, users can identify and extract variables across waves and studies within standardized conceptual frameworks and generate tailored documentation to support transparent, reproducible workflows. We present a use case demonstrating metadata-driven, variable-level access for longitudinal data preparation and cross-study comparison.  The portal provides concept-oriented, variable-level discovery and extraction that streamlines identification of comparable measures, supports cross-wave assessment of measurement continuity, and reduces technical and cognitive burdens associated with assembling longitudinal analytic files. The use case illustrates how variable-level access and autogenerated documentation facilitate efficient dataset construction and reproducible analysis pipelines.  By shifting from file-centric dissemination to harmonized, concept-based metadata and variable-level extraction, the NACDA Portal lowers barriers to longitudinal and cross-study aging research. This approach can strengthen transparency, comparability, and reproducibility, supporting cumulative science as aging data resources continue to grow.

reviewRecords.title: Human Capital and Developmental Strengths: Older Adults and the Implementation of Age-Friendly Community Initiatives
reviewRecords.abstract: and  Discourse on age-friendly communities (AFCs) calls for the meaningful inclusion of older adults as partners and contributors to community-change processes. Nevertheless, there has been very little theoretical or empirical attention as to why older adults’ involvement matters. Our study aimed to address this gap by exploring the strengths-based qualities that older adults bring as implementation actors in AFC initiatives. Research Design and  We conducted a secondary analysis of qualitative interview data from 23 older adults across four states in the United States about their experiences leading or partnering on the implementation of AFC initiatives (e.g., as an AFC committee chair or workgroup member). We engaged in iterative rounds of coding and analytic memo writing using abductive qualitative analysis.  Three thematic categories emerged regarding qualities that older adults bring to AFC implementation processes: (a) accumulated knowledge of aging and the community (based on prior professional and life experiences, as well as long-time residency in the community), (b) continuity of specialized skills and abilities (such as volunteer management, integrative thinking, and entrepreneurial skills), and (c) values extension and congruence with the AFC initiative (valuing older adults and the community, as well as valuing the psychosocial opportunities of participation).  We situate our findings within the broader theoretical concepts of human capital and developmental strengths. We discuss how these theoretical orientations can promote the design of more optimal opportunities for older adults’ civic contributions through AFC initiatives, with strong potential to benefit individuals and communities alike.

reviewRecords.title: How aging shapes interoception: A multimodal, multidimensional analysis
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Aging is known to influence perceptual sensitivity, yet its effects on interoception across the lifespan remain poorly understood. Prior research has largely focused on single interoceptive dimensions (e.g., interoceptive sensitivity) or modalities (e.g., cardiac interoception). Moreover, most studies have assessed interoception at rest, limiting insight into how individuals track real-time changes in interoceptive state. In this study, we examined age-related differences in both interoceptive sensitivity and sensibility across cardiac and respiratory modalities in healthy adults.  In a single session, participants (N = 78; aged 18-79 years; M age = 49.10) were assessed for: 1) interoceptive sensibility using the Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness (Version 2); 2) cardiac interoceptive awareness using a heartbeat tapping task under baseline and breath-holding perturbations; and 3) respiratory interoceptive awareness using an inspiratory load estimation task with varying resistance levels. Using the non-invasive interoceptive perturbations, we elicited dynamic fluctuations in interoceptive signals. Associations between age-related differences in interoceptive awareness measures were examined using linear mixed-effects models.  Our  revealed that older age was associated with reduced cardiac interoceptive sensitivity during breath-holding, while respiratory sensitivity remained stable across ages. Additionally, interoceptive sensibility increased with age, suggesting that task-based interoceptive performance and self-reported sensibility may follow divergent aging pathways. Discussion These findings demonstrate that interoceptive awareness does not decline uniformly with age but instead varies by modality and dimension. By identifying how aging differentially impacts interoceptive sensitivity and sensibility across systems, this study opens new avenues for characterizing age-related changes in interoceptive awareness and bodily regulation.

reviewRecords.title: The Respective Roles of Negative and Positive Views of Aging in Predicting Rehabilitation Outcomes
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Subjective views of aging (VoA) predict health outcomes, yet most studies rely on specific measures of VoA in relatively healthy samples. Referring to multidimensional (generalized and personal) and multidirectional (negative and positive) VoA constructs, we examined whether these VoA differentially predict rehabilitation outcomes among older adult patients coping with hip fracture and stroke.  One hundred and fifty-eight geriatric rehabilitation patients (mean age=77.15, SD=6.71) reported VoA at admission while referring to negative and positive generalized (Attitudes to Aging Questionnaire, AAQ) and personal views (awareness of age-related changes, AARC). Patients' functional independence was evaluated by healthcare personnel at admission and discharge, and rehabilitation efficiency (RE) was computed to reflect functional improvement relative to potential. Path analyses tested the unique contributions of negative and positive VoA (for both generalized and personal views) while adjusting for other predictors of RE.  For both generalized and personal VoA, negative views (i.e., AAQ-Losses and AARC-Losses) predicted lower RE, whereas positive views (i.e., AAQ-growth and AARC-Gains) did not show significant effects on RE. Negative views had a significantly stronger effect on RE than positive views, but only for the AAQ subscales. Discussion In the rehabilitation context, negative VoA, referring to age-related losses, appear more consequential for functional recovery than positive VoA (referring to age-related growth and gains). Findings support prioritizing interventions that identify and modify both generalized and personal attitudes, especially those focused on age-related losses, during rehabilitation to enhance functional outcomes.

reviewRecords.title: Past-Month Tobacco and Cannabis Co-Use by Chronic Disease and Sociodemographic Factors Among U.S. Adults 65+ Years (2021-2023)
reviewRecords.abstract: Tobacco and cannabis co-use prevalence is rising, with older adults disproportionately impacted.  Assess tobacco and cannabis co-use by health and sociodemographic characteristics among adults 65+ years.  Using National Survey on Drug Use and Health nationally representative data (2021-2023), we estimated past-month tobacco and cannabis co-use prevalence among adults 65+ years ( N = 15,672). Multinomial logistic regressions examined associations between health and sociodemographic characteristics with past-month co-use, tobacco-only use, and cannabis-only use (vs. former use).  One in six reported past-month use of either cannabis or tobacco (1.7% co-used). More chronic disease diagnoses was associated with lower co-use (e.g., one vs. none: adjusted relative risk ratio [aRRR] = 0.47). Co-use was higher among people with worse self-rated health (e.g., fair/poor vs. excellent/very good: aRRR = 2.73) and past-year mental illness (aRRR = 2.07).  Clinicians working with older adults should account for cannabis co-use in tobacco cessation and disseminate evidence-based cannabis information.

reviewRecords.title: Advancing the Evidence Base for Adult Day Services: A New Five-Year Research Agenda for 2026–2031
reviewRecords.abstract: Adult day services (ADS) provide care and social support for adults with complex health needs, yet they remain an understudied long-term care sector whose impact on patient outcomes is unclear.  To inform an updated research agenda that supports a coordinated approach to measuring impact of ADS and gaps in services in an evolving policy landscape.  We convened 32 stakeholders in partnership with the National Adult Day Services Association. Following a pre-convening evidence review, a facilitated discussion took place. Rapid qualitative synthesis of notes was used to identify themes and consensus priorities.  Participants’ priority was strengthening data infrastructure. They wished to leverage data to identify workforce shortages, implement evidence-based interventions, advance policymaker understanding of ADS, and address uneven reimbursements. The agenda prioritizes standardizing outcome measures, supporting workforce capacity, and translating research into policy. These stakeholder-informed priorities can guide research and policy to demonstrate impact and expand access to ADS.

reviewRecords.title: A generalized approach for estimating the pace of aging
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Quantifying the rate of aging is essential for understanding age-related physiological decline and predicting late-life outcomes. The Pace of Aging (PoA) framework addresses this by modeling longitudinal changes across multiple biomarkers. However, the original Dunedin PoA assigns equal weight to all biomarkers and was derived from a young cohort with limited mortality follow-up, which restricts its applicability in older populations and in settings where biomarker relevance is uncertain.  We developed a weighted Pace of Aging (wPoA) using data from the Swedish Adoption/Twin Study of Aging (SATSA), a longitudinal cohort of older adults with up to nine waves of biomarker data collected over three decades. Using mixed effects models, we estimated individual random intercepts and slopes for 10 biomarkers and assigned weights to these random effects based on their association with time-to-mortality. This mortality-informed weighting distinguishes the wPoA from the original Dunedin PoA.  We found that wPoA was positively correlated with established biological age predictors and more strongly correlated with low-dimensional predictors such as Functional Aging Index (FAA) and the Frailty Index (FI). Modest correlations across all considered predictors suggest that each measure captures distinct aspects of biological aging.  In , the wPoA framework introduces a data-driven weighting of random effects and is particularly well-suited for aging cohorts and in settings where marker relevance is uncertain a priori, such as high-dimensional or omics-based contexts. This work provides a foundation for future single-timepoint surrogates that can also be used in settings lacking rich longitudinal data.

reviewRecords.title: Effect of an Intersectoral Telemedicine Intervention on Hospitalization in Nursing Home Patients: Specification Curve Analysis of a Stepped Wedge Cluster Randomized Trial
reviewRecords.abstract: The use of emergency medical services in Germany has significantly increased, particularly for nonemergency cases. This issue becomes especially relevant for nursing homes, where staff is confronted with resource shortages and organizational challenges, making emergency medical services involvement a common course of action. This leads to potentially avoidable hospitalizations for nursing home residents and exposes them to severe health risks, such as nosocomial infections. To address this, we developed the Optimal@NRW project, implementing an innovative intersectoral telemedicine intervention that includes an early warning system and mobile nonphysician medical assistants in order to enable outpatient treatment in acute medical cases for nursing home residents. We hypothesize that hospitalizations could be significantly reduced, as patients could be treated on-site in the absence of a life-threatening emergency.  This study aims to determine the effect of an intersectoral telemedicine-based intervention for acute care situations on hospitalization among residents in nursing homes.  We conducted a prospective multicenter cluster-randomized stepped wedge trial from May 2021 to April 2023 across 24 nursing homes in western Germany. Nursing homes were randomly assigned to one of four sequences and followed over eight 3-month periods. All sequences crossed stepwise from the control to the intervention phase. We collected primary data in an electronic patient record and claims data from statutory health insurance funds. In a specification curve analysis, we evaluated the intervention effect using multiple mixed-effects regression model specifications with varying modeling approaches, datasets, dependent and independent variables, and operationalizations.  The number of participants ranged from 158 to 285 nursing home residents per sequence and period, totaling 1151 participants in the control phase and 1271 participants in the intervention phase. A total of 1260 regression models were analyzed. Approximately two-thirds of all models exhibited a negative (ie, protective) intervention effect. However, no models exhibited a statistically significant (ie, P  Our  do not support the hypothesis of a significant reduction of hospitalizations among nursing home residents. The effectiveness of the intervention may have been compromised by external factors such as a flood disaster in the study region and the COVID-19 pandemic, which introduced unforeseen challenges. Future studies should prioritize targeted outcomes (potentially avoidable hospitalizations) that align with the specific intervention mechanism, while also allowing for extended implementation periods to ensure that interventions reach their full potential.

reviewRecords.title: construction and evaluation of sarcopenia risk prediction model for non-obese older adults
reviewRecords.abstract: Introduction: Sarcopenia is common in older adults, with distinct features in non-obese individuals. This study developed and validated a nomogram to predict sarcopenia risk specifically in non-obese older adults. : Data from 1,654 CHARLS participants were used for model development and internal validation, and 263 NHANES participants for external validation. LASSO regression selected predictors. A nomogram was constructed and assessed using AUC (discrimination), calibration curves (accuracy), and decision curve analysis (clinical utility). : Seven variables were included in the final nomogram: age, sex, BMI, hemoglobin (Hb), difficulty rising from a chair, history of falls, and basic living ability. The model demonstrated excellent discrimination, with an AUC of 0.88 (95% CI: 0.86-0.90) in the training set. Performance remained robust in the internal (AUC 0.89, 95% CI: 0.85-0.92) and external (AUC 0.94, 95% CI: 0.91-0.97) validation sets. In the sex-stratified analysis, age, BMI, BUN, liver diseases, and basic living ability were included in the male model (AUC: 0.95, 95% CI: 0.93-0.97). For females, age, BMI, creatinine (Cr), difficulty running 1 km, and basic living ability were included (AUC: 0.83, 95% CI: 0.79-0.87). All models demonstrated good calibration and clinical utility. : This study established an effective and simple prediction model for sarcopenia in non-obese older adults. This nomogram can serve as a valuable clinical tool for the early identification and proactive management of sarcopenia in this specific population.
